unit.title: Follow principles of Occupational Health and Safety (OH&S) in work environment

theory1.instructions: Answer all 45 questions. Each question has one best answer: choose it. Each question is worth 1 mark. Time allowed: 2 hours 30 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

questions.stem: A maintenance task on a distribution board is often done live. Which change is the most effective control?
options: Give the worker thicker rubber gloves to wear
Plan it so the board is isolated first
Put up a sign warning everyone else to keep away
Ask a second person to watch the worker

questions.stem: Which of these is an engineering control against electric shock?
options: A toolbox talk about shock
A permit-to-work system
Insulating gloves and mats
RCD protection on outlets

questions.stem: A risk assessment for rewiring an occupied house rates "contact with live parts" as high. Which control should be put in place first?
options: Isolate and lock off before any work on circuits
Remind the team to be extra careful near any live parts
Keep a first-aid kit in the van
Work faster to cut the time exposed

questions.stem: Why can an arc flash at a large main switchboard be more dangerous than one at a small house board?
options: The main switchboard has a lower voltage
Breakers at large boards never trip
Much higher fault current can flow there
Large boards are usually kept outdoors

questions.stem: What clothing should be worn where there is a risk of arc flash?
options: Polyester overalls, as they are light and cool
A cotton T-shirt with a nylon jacket on top
Arc-rated clothing suited to the hazard
Shorts and a vest to stay cool in the heat

questions.stem: A scissor lift must be used under overhead power lines in a car park. What is the first step?
options: Get the safe distance, asking the power company
Raise it slowly and stop when it touches the line
Use it only on a dry day, as rain makes lines live
Wrap the lift's rails in tape to insulate them

questions.stem: Why must a standby generator be connected through a proper changeover (transfer) switch?
options: So the generator uses less fuel at night
So the house can run both supplies at once
So the generator's noise is reduced
So it cannot feed back into the power lines

questions.stem: Why are the DC cables from solar panels treated as live even when the inverter is switched off?
options: The inverter stores power for many days after
The panels make voltage whenever light falls on them
DC cables are always connected straight to the mains
The panels only work at night

questions.stem: Why must a room where lead-acid batteries are charged be well ventilated?
options: Charging can give off hydrogen, which can explode
The batteries need fresh air to hold their charge
Cool air makes the batteries charge twice as fast
The acid needs oxygen to stay liquid

questions.stem: Battery acid splashes into a worker's eye. What should be done first?
options: Rub the eye gently to remove the acid
Cover the eye with a pad and wait for the doctor
Rinse with clean water for at least 15–20 minutes
Put some eye drops in and carry on working as usual

questions.stem: A large motor drive has been isolated. Why should you wait and test before touching its terminals?
options: The motor may still be hot from running
Its capacitors can stay charged for some minutes
The drive needs time to save its settings
The cable needs to cool before it is moved

questions.stem: While removing an old board in a building from the 1970s, you find a grey fibrous sheet behind it. What should you do?
options: Break it up and bag it with the other rubbish
Sand it smooth so the new board fits better
Sweep up any dust and carry on with the job
Stop, keep people away and report it for testing

questions.stem: You must run cable across a roof with fragile sheets. What is the safest approach?
options: Walk only on the sheets that look strong
Spread your weight by crawling on the sheets
Work quickly so you are on the roof less time
Use crawl boards and fall protection

questions.stem: Which is the safest way to work for two hours on light fittings 4 m above a warehouse floor?
options: A long ladder leaned against the racking
A mobile tower or lift with guard rails
Standing on a pallet raised by a forklift
A stepladder placed on top of a table

questions.stem: Your team is laying cable in a trench that is getting deep, in soft soil. What is the main danger?
options: The cable may be too long for the trench
The soil may be too dry to backfill
The sides may collapse and bury someone
Water pipes may be laid in it later on

questions.stem: A cable pit is deep, has one small opening and has been closed for months. Before anyone goes in, what is needed?
options: A trained team, an atmosphere test and a rescue plan
A torch and a mobile phone for the person going in
Only a quick look down from the top of the opening
A fan blowing into the pit for one minute

questions.stem: How should a heavy cable drum be set up when cable is pulled off it?
options: Roll it along the floor while pulling the cable
Mount it on drum jacks or a stand with a spindle
Stand it on its side and lift the cable off the top
Have one person sit on it to keep it still

questions.stem: Your team is working in a hot roof space in August. Which plan best reduces the risk of heat illness?
options: Work early, take shaded breaks and drink water often
Work straight through to finish before lunch
Drink sweet energy drinks instead of water to keep going
Wear fewer clothes and no PPE to stay cool

questions.stem: PVC solvent cement is used to join conduit in a small room. What precaution is needed?
options: Use it near a heater so it dries faster
Pour unused cement down the drain
Ventilate the room and keep flames away
Leave the tin open so it does not go hard

questions.stem: Before using insulating gloves, what should an electrician check?
options: That they are a bright colour and easy for others to see
That they are loose enough to come off quickly
That they have been washed in hot water
That they are in date and have no holes or cracks

questions.stem: A trainee says the job is behind and asks to change an outlet live, "just this once", to save time. What should you do?
options: Refuse, and plan the work so it is done dead
Agree, as long as you stand beside the trainee
Agree, but tell them to wear gloves
Leave the decision to the trainee

questions.stem: An electrician gets a shock from a board that was marked as isolated. Which cause is most worth finding?
options: The electrician was unlucky on the day
The weather was hot and humid
The board was painted the wrong colour
Why the board's labels and isolation were wrong

questions.stem: Which shows a good safety culture in an electrical contractor's team?
options: Near misses are hidden to keep the record clean
Anyone can stop a job they think is unsafe
Only the manager may talk about safety
Safety rules are skipped when the job is late

questions.stem: A team leader sees a worker from another firm using a damaged extension lead on your site. What should the team leader do?
options: Ignore it, as the worker is not in their team
Take a photo to use against the other firm later
Stop it politely and tell the site manager
Borrow the lead and test it themselves

questions.stem: A worker is found unresponsive beside an open distribution board. What should you do first?
options: Pull them away by the arm straight away
Pour water on them to wake them up
Check for danger and cut the supply
Wait for someone else to arrive and decide

questions.stem: After a shock, the casualty is not breathing normally. Once help has been called, what is right?
options: Give them a cool drink of water and fan them
Start CPR and use an AED if one is available
Leave them lying alone until the ambulance comes
Sit them up and ask them to walk around

questions.stem: Which is correct first aid for an electrical burn on the hand, once the casualty is safe?
options: Cool it with running water and cover with cling film
Put butter or cooking oil on it to keep the air out
Burst any blisters so the burn can dry
Wrap it tightly in a dry, fluffy cotton towel

questions.stem: Why should cable offcuts and packaging not be left to build up in a plant room?
options: They make the room look untidy to the client
They attract mosquitoes in the rainy season
They stop the air conditioning from working
They are fuel for a fire and a trip hazard

questions.stem: Why should the team know where the nearest isolator, first-aid kit and AED are before work starts?
options: So they can borrow them for other jobs
So the client can be charged for them
So they do not need any first-aid training
So no time is lost in an emergency

questions.stem: A new electrician joins your site team today. What must happen before they start work?
options: A site induction: hazards, rules, emergencies
A long lunch to get to know the team
A test of how fast they can wire a board
Nothing, if they have worked on sites before

questions.stem: An electrician must work alone in a remote pump house. Which control is most important?
options: Take extra tools along in case of any problems
Finish quickly and leave before dark
Agree check-in calls and action if missed
Bring a radio for music to stay alert

questions.stem: Why should temporary lighting in a wet trench or tank run from a safety extra-low voltage supply?
options: So the lamps last longer in damp places
To cut the shock risk in wet conditions
So the lamps give off less heat in the trench
To make the lights cheaper to run each day

questions.stem: A board must be left open for a short time while your team fetches parts. What should be done?
options: Leave it, as long as you are back quickly
Close it, or barrier it and leave a person
Put a cardboard box in front of it
Ask the client's children to keep watch

questions.stem: During a site inspection you find a temporary supply lead running through standing water. What should you do?
options: Note it on the form and check it next week
Move it with your bare hands to a dry spot
Have it isolated, then reroute or replace it
Cover the water with a sheet of plywood

questions.stem: Why should a team leader carry out regular site safety inspections with a checklist?
options: To find people to blame for problems
To fill in time when work is slow
To make the site look busy to the client
To find hazards early and check controls work

questions.stem: Burning PVC cable gives off thick black smoke. Why is it so dangerous?
options: It contains toxic and corrosive gases
It makes the fire burn without oxygen
It puts the fire out but stains walls
It is harmless but smells unpleasant

questions.stem: Rat droppings are found in a ceiling void where cables must be run. What precaution is needed?
options: Gloves, a mask and wet cleaning, then wash
Sweep the droppings away with a dry broom
Blow them out with compressed air first
Ignore them, as they are only a nuisance

questions.stem: A team member arrives smelling of alcohol and is unsteady on his feet. What should the team leader do?
options: Let him work, but only on ladders
Give him coffee and let him carry on
Ignore it so as not to embarrass him
Stop him working and report it

questions.stem: Why should workers be involved when a new safe work procedure is written?
options: So the procedure can be written faster
They know the real job and its hazards
So the supervisor has less responsibility
So the procedure needs no later review

questions.stem: Why must the earth conductor of a temporary site supply be checked, not just the live parts?
options: So the site lighting is much brighter at night
So the meter records less of the energy used
So a fault trips the supply, not leaving metal live
So the cables are easier to coil up after use

questions.stem: Your team is laying cable beside a driveway used by delivery trucks. What control is needed?
options: Work faster whenever trucks are coming
Wear dark clothes so drivers are not distracted
Barriers, signs and high-visibility clothing
Park the van across the drive to stop all traffic

questions.stem: After a repair, a circuit is ready to be switched back on. What must happen first?
options: Tests pass, all clear, each owner removes their lock
The client switches it on to save time
The breaker is switched on and off quickly to check it
The tags are thrown away so nobody gets confused

questions.stem: A worker is very tired after several 14-hour days. Why is this a safety issue?
options: Tired workers always work more slowly
The client will not pay for tired workers
Tiredness only matters when driving
Tired people make more mistakes

questions.stem: Which events should be reported at work?
options: Only those injuries that need a hospital visit
All injuries, near misses and unsafe conditions
Only those that someone else saw happen
Only those that damage tools or materials

questions.stem: After an incident report, what should the team leader do with the actions agreed?
options: File them away and wait for the next incident
Read them out once and then forget them
Give each an owner and date, then check them
Send them only to the client

theory2.instructions: Section A has 15 short answers (2 marks each). Section B has 10 essay questions (5 marks each): answer each in full sentences. Time allowed: 3 hours 35 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

shortAnswers.stem: What name is given to the order of control measures, from elimination down to PPE?
What is the name of the fibrous mineral, found in some old buildings and boards, whose dust can cause lung cancer?
What is the name of the device that takes several padlocks, so that several workers can each lock the same isolator?
What is the name of the system of boards, struts or boxes used to stop the sides of a trench falling in?
What do we call current that flows from a building's generator back into the power company's lines?
What is the name of the quick check in which insulating gloves are rolled up from the cuff to trap air and show any leaks?
Electrical burns can look small on the skin. What may they hide underneath?
What one word is used for an insulating cover fitted over nearby live parts to stop accidental contact?
What word describes a roof material that would break if a person stepped on it, such as old fibre-cement or clear sheets?
What is the term for energy left in equipment after it is isolated, such as charge in capacitors or a compressed spring?
Which acidic gas, given off by burning PVC, harms the lungs and corrodes metal?
What do we call the person who stays outside a confined space to keep watch and raise the alarm?
What do we call the equipment, such as a harness and lanyard tied to an anchor, that stops a falling worker from hitting the ground?
What do we call a planned walk round the site with a checklist to find hazards and check controls?
What heat illness, with heavy sweating, cramps, weakness and dizziness, can come before heat stroke?

essays.stem: Your team will replace the main distribution board in a shop that stays open on the other side of a partition. Identify the main hazards and describe the controls you would use, working down the hierarchy of controls.
essays.modelAnswer: The main hazards are electric shock and arc flash from live parts, especially the incoming supply side, which stays live until the power company or a competent person isolates it. Others are manual handling of the heavy board, dust and noise from drilling, sharp edges, fire, and members of the public walking into the work area. Working down the hierarchy: first, eliminate live work by arranging a full shutdown and isolation of the supply, and plan the job so no circuit is worked on live. Substitute cordless tools to remove trailing leads. Use engineering controls: lock off, shroud any parts that stay live, fit barriers around the work area, and use dust extraction. Administrative controls include a method statement, a permit where needed, personal locks and tags, signs, a briefing, and agreed working times with the shop. Finally, PPE: safety boots, glasses, gloves, and arc-rated clothing where any live part is near.
markingPoints: Identifies shock and arc flash, including the live supply side
Identifies other hazards: handling, dust, noise, public
Elimination: full isolation, no live work
Engineering and administrative controls: locks, shrouds, barriers, permits, briefing
PPE named as the last line of defence

essays.stem: Four electricians will work on different circuits of the same board at the same time. Describe how you would manage isolation for the whole team, from start to switch-on.
essays.modelAnswer: I would plan the isolation from the drawings and identify every source of supply, including any generator or solar system. I switch off and isolate the board at its main isolator and any other source. Each electrician fits their own padlock and danger tag, with their name and date, either on the isolator with a multi-lock hasp or on a group lock box that holds the isolator key. Nobody removes another person's lock. I check my two-pole tester on a proving unit, prove the board dead at the point of work on all conductors, and prove the tester again. I check for stored energy, such as capacitors. Any parts that stay live are shrouded and signed. If someone leaves and returns, they test again. At the end, each person confirms their work is finished, tools are out and covers are on, and removes only their own lock. I check all locks are off and everyone is clear, announce the switch-on, and record it.
markingPoints: Identifies all sources of supply
Each person fits own lock and tag (hasp or lock box)
Proves dead with a tester checked before and after
Deals with stored energy and parts that stay live
Controlled switch-on: work complete, own locks removed, all clear, announced

essays.stem: Explain what an arc flash is, what can cause one, what harm it can do, and how the risk is controlled.
essays.modelAnswer: An arc flash is a sudden release of energy when current jumps through the air between conductors or from a conductor to earth. It makes intense heat, bright light, a pressure blast, flying molten metal and loud noise in a fraction of a second. It can be caused by a dropped tool or loose part touching live conductors, by testing with the wrong meter or damaged leads, by dust, damp or vermin in switchgear, or by operating faulty equipment. The harm includes severe burns, eye damage, hearing loss, injuries from the blast and fires, and it can kill. The best control is to work dead, with the supply isolated. Where that is not possible, only competent people do the work, under a permit, with the right meter and leads, insulated tools, and shrouds over nearby parts. People keep back from the equipment, and the worker wears arc-rated clothing and face protection suited to the hazard. Good maintenance of switchgear also lowers the risk.
markingPoints: Describes arc flash: energy through air, heat, light, blast
Gives causes: dropped tools, wrong meters, faulty or dirty gear
Describes harm: burns, eyes, hearing, blast, fire, death
Main control: work dead
Other controls: competent people, permits, right tools, shrouds, distance, arc-rated PPE, maintenance

essays.stem: Your team will fit solar panels and run their cables on the roof of a house in St Elizabeth. Describe the hazards and how you would control them.
essays.modelAnswer: The main hazards are falls from the roof edge or through fragile parts of the roof, falling objects, heat and sun, and electrical hazards. Before work, I would check the roof's condition and whether any part is fragile. Falls are controlled with edge protection or scaffold, or, where that cannot be used, a harness and lanyard attached to a suitable anchor, with a rescue plan. Crawl boards are used on fragile areas, and safe access is provided by a secured ladder or scaffold. Tools and materials are tied or kept in trays, and the area below is fenced off. Work is planned for the cooler morning, with shade, water and breaks to prevent heat illness, and wind and rain are checked. Solar panels make voltage whenever light falls on them, so their DC cables are treated as live: connectors are kept apart until the end, and the panels may be covered. Panels are lifted with care by two people.
markingPoints: Falls controlled: edge protection, scaffold or harness with rescue plan
Fragile roof and safe access controlled
Falling objects: tools secured, area below fenced
Heat and weather managed
Panels treated as live in daylight; safe handling of panels

essays.stem: Describe how you would plan and control the safety of digging a 25 m trench for an underground cable on a busy commercial site.
essays.modelAnswer: First I would check the site plans for buried services and ask the owner and service providers, then scan the route with a cable and pipe detector and mark any services found. Near marked services, the team digs by hand. I would plan how deep the trench will be and whether its sides need support. Soft or deep trenches must be shored or have their sides sloped, so nobody is buried by a collapse. Spoil is kept back from the edge so it cannot fall in or overload the sides, and plant is kept away from the edge. The trench is fenced with barriers and signs, and covered or lit if left overnight, so people and vehicles cannot fall in. A banksman guides any digger, and the team wears high-visibility clothing. Safe ways in and out of the trench are provided, and water is pumped out. I would check the trench each day and after rain before anyone enters.
markingPoints: Checks plans, scans and marks services; hand digs near them
Supports or slopes the sides against collapse
Spoil and plant kept back from the edge
Barriers, signs, cover or lighting; vehicle control and hi-vis
Safe access, water removed, daily checks

essays.stem: Describe the hazards of a lead-acid battery bank for a standby or solar system, and the controls and first aid needed.
essays.modelAnswer: Lead-acid batteries hold a lot of energy. A short circuit across their terminals, for example from a dropped spanner, can cause a large spark, burns and melted metal, and they cannot be switched off like the mains. When charging, they can give off hydrogen, which can explode if it builds up and meets a spark. They contain sulphuric acid, which burns skin and eyes. They are also very heavy. Controls: the battery room is well ventilated and kept free of flames and sparks, with no smoking. Insulated tools are used, rings and watches are removed, and terminals are covered. Connections are made in the order the maker gives, with the battery isolators open. Batteries are lifted with help or a trolley. Workers wear eye protection, gloves and an apron. An eye wash station and water are kept nearby. If acid gets into the eyes or on the skin, rinse with plenty of clean water for at least 15 minutes and get medical help.
markingPoints: Short-circuit energy and burns; cannot be switched off
Hydrogen explosion risk when charging
Acid burns and heavy weight
Controls: ventilation, no flames, insulated tools, covered terminals, maker's order, PPE
First aid: rinse with plenty of water and get medical help

essays.stem: An electrician received a shock while working on a circuit that was labelled as isolated. Describe how you would investigate the incident and prevent it happening again.
essays.modelAnswer: First I make sure the injured person gets medical care and the area is made safe: the circuit is truly isolated, locked off and proved dead. I keep the scene as it was where possible and take photos. I report the incident as the company and the law require. I then talk to the injured person and any witnesses soon, separately, while memories are fresh, and without blame. I collect the facts: the drawings and labels, the isolation record, which breaker was switched off, whether the circuit was proved dead and with what tester, and whether the tester was checked. I compare what happened with the safe isolation procedure. I look for the root cause, for example a board labelled wrongly after an earlier change, a second supply, or a step of the procedure skipped because of time pressure. Then actions are agreed, such as relabelling, training, and changing the procedure, each with a name and a date. I check they are done and share the lessons with the team.
markingPoints: Care for the injured and make the area safe
Preserve the scene, photograph and report
Interview people promptly and without blame; gather documents
Compare with the procedure and find the root cause
Agree actions with owners and dates, follow up and share lessons

essays.stem: Explain the OH&S duties of the employer, the team leader and each worker on an electrical job, and describe what a team leader should do if a worker refuses to do a task they believe is unsafe.
essays.modelAnswer: The employer must provide a safe workplace, safe equipment and tools, training, information, PPE, safe systems of work such as isolation procedures, and first aid, and must assess risks. The team leader plans work safely, briefs the team, makes sure procedures are followed, checks tools and PPE, supervises trainees, stops unsafe work and reports incidents. Each worker must follow the procedures and training, use PPE and equipment properly, look after their own safety and that of others, and report hazards, near misses and incidents. If a worker refuses a task they think is unsafe, the team leader should stop that task, thank them for raising it, and listen to the concern without pressure or threats. The leader should look at the hazard with them, check the risk assessment, and either fix the problem, change the method, or get advice. Work only restarts when it is safe and the worker is satisfied. The concern and the action taken are recorded.
markingPoints: Employer duties: safe place, equipment, training, PPE, systems, risk assessment
Team leader duties: plan, brief, supervise, enforce, report
Worker duties: follow procedures, use PPE, care for others, report
Refusal: stop the task, listen without pressure
Investigate and fix before restarting; record

essays.stem: Describe what an emergency plan for an electrical contractor's site team should cover, and how you would make sure the team is ready to use it.
essays.modelAnswer: The plan should cover the emergencies most likely on an electrical job: electric shock, burns, falls from height, fire, serious cuts and someone collapsing in the heat. For each, it should say what to do first, who does what, and how to call for help, including the emergency numbers and the site address or directions for the ambulance. It should show where the main isolators are, so the supply can be cut quickly, and where the first-aid kit, AED, fire extinguishers and eye wash are. It should name trained first-aiders and fire wardens, and give the assembly point. It should include a rescue plan for anyone working at height or in a confined space. To make sure the team is ready, I would explain the plan at the site induction, put copies where everyone can see them, check equipment regularly, and run drills, such as a shock-rescue or evacuation practice. After each drill or real event, the plan is reviewed and improved.
markingPoints: Covers likely emergencies: shock, burns, falls, fire, heat
Actions, roles and how to call help with the site address
Locations of isolators, first aid, AED, extinguishers; named first-aiders and wardens
Rescue plans for height and confined spaces
Induction, displayed copies, equipment checks, drills and review

essays.stem: While rewiring an old school building, your team finds dust and broken boards that might contain asbestos. Explain what you would do and why.
essays.modelAnswer: I would stop the work in that area at once and tell everyone to move away without disturbing the material further, because asbestos fibres are released when it is broken, drilled or swept, and breathing them in can cause lung cancer and other diseases many years later. I would close off the area with barriers and signs so nobody enters. I would not try to clean it up, sweep it or use a normal vacuum, which would spread the fibres. I would report it to my supervisor and the school, and ask for the material to be tested by a qualified person. If it is asbestos, only trained, licensed or approved specialists may remove it, following the rules. I would record who was in the area and for how long, in case of future health checks. Work would only restart in that area when it has been made safe and cleared. I would also check the plan for other old parts of the building before drilling there.
markingPoints: Stops work and moves people away; explains fibre risk
Closes off the area with barriers and signs
Does not clean or disturb it
Reports and gets it tested; removal only by specialists
Records exposure; restarts only when cleared; checks other areas

practical1.title: Risk assessment, method statement and team isolation for a board change
practical1.brief: The assessor gives the group a scenario: four electricians will replace outgoing circuits on a board in a small workshop. As a group: (1) carry out a risk assessment of the job, scoring each hazard before and after controls, and list the controls in hierarchy order; (2) write a short method statement and isolation plan; (3) on a training board NOT connected to any supply, carry out the team isolation: switch off, fit a multi-lock hasp or group lock box, each member fits their own padlock and danger tag, prove dead with a two-pole tester checked on a proving unit before and after, shroud and sign parts treated as live, and fence off the area; (4) carry out the switch-on procedure: each member confirms their work is complete and removes only their own lock, and the leader announces the switch-on. Members take turns as leader and as tester.
materials: Scenario sheet and risk assessment and method statement forms
Training board NOT connected to any supply
Multi-lock hasp or group lock box, a padlock and danger tag for each member
Two-pole voltage indicator and proving unit
Insulating shrouds, barriers and warning signs
PPE: safety glasses, insulating gloves for inspection, boots
photos: The completed risk assessment with scores before and after controls
The method statement and isolation plan
The hasp or lock box with every member's lock and tag
The tester being proved on the proving unit before and after the test for dead
Shrouds, barriers and signs in place
The switch-on: locks removed by their owners and the leader's check sheet
checklist: Identified realistic hazards and scored them sensibly
Chose controls in the right order of the hierarchy
Fitted and removed only their own lock and tag
Proved dead correctly with the tester checked before and after
Set up shrouds, barriers and signs correctly
Took a turn as leader or tester and gave clear instructions
safety: The training board is never connected to a supply in this task
Treat every step as real: no shortcuts with locks, tags or testing
Check insulating gloves and PPE before use
Keep the work area clear and fenced

practical2.title: Site safety inspection, toolbox talk and emergency drill
practical2.brief: The assessor sets up a mock electrical work site at the Centre with several planted hazards (for example a damaged lead, a lead through water, an open board, a poorly set ladder, an unguarded trench mock-up, a battery area with no eye wash). As a group: (1) plan and carry out a safety inspection with a checklist, photograph each hazard, rate its risk and propose controls; (2) write an inspection report with actions, owners and dates; (3) one or two members give a 10-minute toolbox talk to the rest on the most serious hazard found; (4) run an emergency drill for an electric shock: make the area safe by isolating (the assessor names the isolator; nothing is live), call for help with the site address, give CPR on a training manikin and use a training AED, and complete an incident report. Each member has a role in each part.
materials: Mock work site with planted hazards (set up by the assessor; nothing live)
Inspection checklist, report and incident report forms
Flip chart for the toolbox talk
photos: The group's inspection plan and checklist
Each hazard found, photographed with its risk rating
The finished inspection report with actions, owners and dates
The drill: area made safe and help called
CPR on the manikin and the training AED in use
checklist: Found and correctly rated at least two hazards
Proposed controls that follow the hierarchy
Wrote clear actions with owners and dates
Took part in or listened actively to the toolbox talk and asked a question
Made the area safe before approaching the casualty in the drill
Called for help with the right information
Did CPR and used the training AED correctly, or supported the person who did
Helped complete an accurate incident report
safety: Nothing in the mock site is live; the assessor confirms this before the start
Do not climb the planted ladder or enter the trench mock-up
Use the manikin and training AED only as the maker says
Report any real hazard you find at once
